blocks.text: A bungee rope, a car bumper and a diving board all do the same job: they store the energy of an impact as elastic strain and give it back. For a bolt struck by a falling tool, how large the stress becomes depends on that energy balance, not on the weight alone, and it can be hundreds of times the static stress.

blocks.markdown: When a load deforms an elastic body, the work it does is stored as **strain energy** $U$ (J, or N mm in mixed units). For a gradually applied load on a linear-elastic body with force $P$ and corresponding displacement $\delta$, $W=\tfrac12P\delta=U$. We assume small deformations, linear-elastic isotropic material, static (slowly applied) loads unless impact is stated, and no energy lost to heat, sound or supports. Energy stored per unit volume under uniaxial stress is $u=\sigma^2/2E$.

blocks.caption: Strain energy for axial, bending and torsional loading (constant section for the axial and torsion forms)

blocks.title: Work-energy equating
blocks.text: For a single load $P$ applied gradually to a linear-elastic structure, the work done is $\tfrac12P\delta$, where $\delta$ is the deflection of the load point **in the direction of the load**. Equating it to the strain energy gives $\delta=2U/P$.

blocks.prompt: A steel bar of cross-section area $A=300$ mm$^2$ and length $L=1.2$ m carries an axial tension $P=25$ kN. Take $E=200$ GPa. Find the strain energy and check it against the work done.

steps.text: Strain energy for a uniform bar.
Work done by the gradually applied load equals the energy.

blocks.title: Deflection of a cantilever tip by equating energy to work
blocks.prompt: A cantilever of square section $40\times40$ mm and length $L=0.8$ m carries a tip load $P=2$ kN. $E=200$ GPa. Find the tip deflection using strain energy.

steps.text: Bending moment at distance $x$ from the tip.
Equate $U=\tfrac12P\delta$ for the tip deflection under the load.

blocks.caption: Strain energy and the deflection it implies (single load, gradually applied)

blocks.markdown: **Impact loading.** A mass $m$ (kg) falling through a height $h$ onto a bar loaded in tension gives up potential energy $mg(h+\delta)$, where $\delta$ is the extension at maximum stretch. All of this is stored as elastic energy $\tfrac12k\delta^2$ with stiffness $k=AE/L$. Solving the quadratic and using $\delta_{st}=mgL/(AE)$ (the static extension under weight $W=mg$) gives the **impact factor**. Assumptions: the bar's own mass is neglected, there is no energy loss, and the stress is uniform (axial wave effects ignored).

blocks.caption: Impact stress; h = drop height measured before the bar begins to stretch. With h = 0 the factor is 2

blocks.title: Impact stress in a bar struck by a falling mass
blocks.prompt: A 15 kg mass falls $h=100$ mm onto a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel rod of area $A=200$ mm$^2$ and length 1.0 m. $E=200$ GPa, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$. Find the maximum stress.

steps.text: Check by energy: $W(h+\delta_{max})=14841.8$ N mm equals $\tfrac12k\delta_{max}^2$ with $\delta_{max}=0.8614$ mm.

blocks.answer: $\sigma_{max}\approx172$ MPa, about 234 times the static stress of 0.74 MPa.

items: Write the load path and find internal forces or moments.
Calculate $U$ with the appropriate integral (axial, bending, torsion) and add contributions from each member.
Equate $U$ to $\tfrac12P\delta$ for a single load, or to the lost potential energy in impact.
Solve for $\delta$ or $\sigma_{max}$ and check it is below yield and that deflection assumptions hold.

blocks.title: Limits of the work-energy method
blocks.text: Equating $U=\tfrac12P\delta$ gives only the displacement at the load point and in the load direction, and only for a single load. For several loads or an unloaded point, use Castigliano or a dummy load.

blocks.title: Energy is additive, forces are not
blocks.text: Total strain energy is the sum of axial, bending and torsional contributions, but because $U$ grows with the **square** of the load, doubling $P$ quadruples $U$.

points: Strain energy is $P^2L/2AE$ for an axial bar and $\int M^2/2EI\,dx$ for bending; for a single gradual load $U=\tfrac12P\delta$.
Equating $U$ to $\tfrac12P\delta$ gives the deflection at the load point in the load direction, for example $PL^3/3EI$ for a cantilever.
Impact: $\sigma_{max}=\sigma_{st}[1+\sqrt{1+2h/\delta_{st}}]$; a suddenly applied load ($h=0$) doubles the stress.
Impact stress is limited by stiffness: a more flexible (longer, thinner) member absorbs the same energy at a lower stress.

questions.stem: A linear-elastic bar is loaded gradually in tension. If the axial load is doubled, the strain energy stored in the bar

options.text: stays the same, since the bar is the same

distractorRationale.b: This would be true only if $U$ were proportional to $P$.
distractorRationale.d: The stored energy depends on the load applied.

questions.explanation: Strain energy $U=P^2L/(2AE)$ is quadratic in the load. Equivalently, both the force and the extension double, so the work $\tfrac12P\delta$ is multiplied by four.

questions.stem: An aluminium bar of area 250 mm$^2$ and length 0.5 m carries a gradually applied axial tension of 40 kN. Taking $E=70$ GPa, calculate the strain energy in joules.
A stepped bar has a 300 mm length of area 400 mm$^2$ followed by a 300 mm length of area 200 mm$^2$. It carries an axial load $P=30$ kN, $E=200$ GPa. The total strain energy is closest to

distractorRationale.a: Drops a term from the sum of $L/A$ contributions, so one segment is undercounted.
distractorRationale.b: Treats both segments as if they had the larger area (0.75 + 0.75), so the thin segment is under-counted.
distractorRationale.c: Doubles the correct value, from forgetting the factor $\tfrac12$ in the denominator.

questions.explanation: Each segment contributes $P^2L_i/(2A_iE)$ and the contributions add. The thinner part stores twice as much energy per unit length, so $U=2250\times(0.75+1.5)=5062$ N mm = 5.06 J.

questions.stem: A simply supported steel beam of span 1.5 m ($E=200$ GPa, $I=8.0\times10^6$ mm$^4$) carries a central point load of 6 kN applied gradually. Using $U=P^2L^3/(96EI)$, calculate the strain energy in joules.
questions.explanation: $U=(6000)^2(1500)^3/(96\times200000\times8.0\times10^6)=791.0$ N mm $=0.791$ J. Equating to $\tfrac12P\delta$ would give a central deflection of $2U/P=0.26$ mm.

questions.stem: Two identical steel bars, each 1.0 m long with area 100 mm$^2$, hang from a ceiling and meet at a joint, each making $30^\circ$ with the vertical (symmetric about the vertical). A vertical load $W=20$ kN is applied gradually at the joint. Taking $E=200$ GPa, find the vertical deflection of the joint in mm by equating strain energy to work.
questions.explanation: Each bar force is $F=W/(2\cos30^\circ)=11547$ N. The total energy is $U=2F^2L/(2AE)=F^2L/(AE)=6666.7$ N mm. Then $\tfrac12W\delta=U$ gives $\delta=2U/W=0.6667$ mm, confirmed by geometry: bar extension $/\cos30^\circ$.

questions.stem: Why can the method of equating strain energy to the work $\tfrac12P\delta$ not be used on its own to find the deflection at a point where no load is applied?

options.text: Strain energy is zero at unloaded points
The only unknown it can give is the displacement of the load point in the direction of the load, because $\tfrac12P\delta$ involves just that one force
The method requires the beam to be statically indeterminate
Strain energy cannot be calculated for beams

questions.correctOptionText: The only unknown it can give is the displacement of the load point in the direction of the load, because $\tfrac12P\delta$ involves just that one force

distractorRationale.a: Strain energy is a property of the whole body and is not zero there.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the work term involves the load and its own displacement only.
distractorRationale.c: The method applies to determinate structures; indeterminacy is a separate issue.
distractorRationale.d: Strain energy can be calculated for beams, as shown for the cantilever.

questions.explanation: The equation $U=\tfrac12P\delta$ is a single scalar equation relating one force to its own displacement. For an unloaded point or for several loads it does not contain enough information, which is why Castigliano's theorem or a dummy load is needed.

questions.stem: A mass of 8 kg falls 50 mm onto a collar at the end of a vertical steel rod of area 120 mm$^2$ and length 0.6 m, $E=200$ GPa, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$. Neglecting the rod's mass and any energy loss, find the maximum stress in the rod in MPa. (Measure the drop before the rod begins to stretch.)
questions.explanation: Static extension is $\delta_{st}=mgL/(AE)=78.48\times600/(120\times200000)=0.001962$ mm and $\sigma_{st}=78.48/120=0.654$ MPa. The impact factor is $1+\sqrt{1+2(50)/0.001962}=226.8$, so $\sigma_{max}=148.3$ MPa.

questions.stem: Explain why a load applied suddenly (released from zero height, $h=0$) produces twice the static stress, and why increasing the length of a bar reduces its impact stress for the same falling mass and height.
markingGuide: With $h=0$ the impact factor is $1+\sqrt{1+0}=2$, so $\sigma_{max}=2\sigma_{st}$.
Energy balance: the load does work $W\delta$ through the full extension but the stored energy is $\tfrac12k\delta^2$, so $\delta=2W/k=2\delta_{st}$.
The bar overshoots the static equilibrium extension by the same amount again; the static state is the midpoint of the oscillation.
Longer bar: lower stiffness $k=AE/L$ and larger $\delta_{st}$, so $2h/\delta_{st}$ falls and the impact factor reduces.
Energy $mgh$ is stored over a larger volume of material, so the energy per unit volume and hence the stress is lower.
questions.explanation: A suddenly applied load does work $W\delta$ while the spring only stores half of that, so the displacement doubles. For a fixed energy input, a more compliant member stores it at lower stress, which is why long thin bolts survive shock better.

questions.stem: A cantilever of length $L=500$ mm has $E=70$ GPa, $I=4.0\times10^5$ mm$^4$ and carries a gradually applied tip load $P=1.5$ kN. Show how to find its tip deflection from strain energy: derive $U$, compute it, and state the deflection. State one limitation of the method.
markingGuide: Moment at distance $x$ from the free end: $M=Px$.
Limitation: gives only the load-point deflection in the load direction, and neglects shear energy (acceptable for slender beams).
questions.explanation: Integrating the squared bending moment over the length gives the energy stored in bending, and equating it to the work done by the single load gives the standard cantilever result $PL^3/3EI$. For multiple loads or deflections elsewhere you need Castigliano's theorem or the unit-load method.

questions.stem: True or false: a weight suddenly released onto a bar with no initial drop height (h = 0) produces a maximum stress twice the static stress.
questions.explanation: With $h=0$ the impact factor $1+\sqrt{1+2h/\delta_{st}}$ equals 2. The load does work through the full extension but the spring only stores half of it at equilibrium, so the bar stretches twice the static value.
